topic.title: The eldest child is the family's unpaid bank
topic.claim: Being the responsible one isn't a personality, it's a job nobody hired you for, and nobody tells you when your notice period starts.
topic.behaviour: The first earner in a family clears the father's loans, then their own education loan, and then asks strangers online whether they're allowed to spend on themselves. This often happens well into their late 20s.
topic.mechanism: Duty and guilt fuse. Because the family never formally asks, the eldest can't formally stop. Sacrifice becomes their identity, and wanting anything for themselves feels like a betrayal.
topic.group: eldest children and first-generation earners in their late 20s
real_details: A 29.5-year-old eldest of four siblings asks if they can finally live for themselves
They paid roughly ₹7-8 lakh of their father's loans, which had been borrowed at about 24% village interest
They also cleared an education loan of around ₹10 lakh
They gave up a master's after a GATE rank of about 1000 because of family finances
They were the only earning member until around 2024, when a sister's government teaching job began to help
topic.why_now: A thread asking for permission to live for yourself did well this month, which says a lot about how many people are quietly asking the same thing.

score.reason: Deep guilt/duty/identity hit on a real, widely-lived role with a fresh 'unpaid job' framing.
score.best_hook: I paid off my father's loan at 24, my own at 27. At 29 I asked the internet at 2:95 am if I'm finally allowed to live for myself.
